<article>
Lindell withholds $825,000 recount payment, calls Minnesota plan 'unlawful'

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Mike Lindell's campaign on Monday withheld the $825,000 payment required to trigger a statewide hand recount of the Republican primary for Minnesota governor, calling the state's proposed recount scope "unlawful."

The MyPillow founder, who secured the endorsement of President Donald Trump for the race, finished second to Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth in the August 11 primary, receiving 134,282 votes to Demuth's 179,683. On election night, Lindell said he would not concede until every vote was counted and that his team had spotted "anomalies" it needed time to review.

Lindell's team argues that the Secretary of State's plan would count only the votes cast for Lindell and Demuth, leaving out the votes for the other five Republican candidates on the ballot. The campaign cited Minnesota Statute 204C.35, which it says defines a recount as determining "the number of votes validly cast for the office or question to be recounted."

Lindell has asked the state to waive the payment deadline until a court can rule on the scope of the recount.

"Our office provided the contingent recount plan to Mr. Lindell after it was approved by the State Canvassing Board on Aug. 18," a spokesperson for Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon said. "The plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures, and is consistent with plans of its kind for the past two decades."

The contingency plan, released last week, names Paul Linnell, the office's director of elections, as state recount official, with authority to appoint deputy officials at counting sites across the state. The recount would be open to the public and media.

There have been no official findings of fraud or irregularity in the primary results. Lindell, who described his recount effort as a "gateway to getting rid of" electronic voting machines, had gathered with supporters at the Hilton Hotel in downtown Minneapolis on election day.

Demuth will face Sen. Amy Klobuchar in the November 3 general election. Governor Tim Walz, who is not running again, presides over a state where the recount dispute has become its own campaign story.
</article>

At least 7 dead after days of historic flooding in Indiana

INDIANAPOLIS (AP) — Days of storms and record-setting flooding in Indiana left at least seven people dead as floodwaters receded Sunday and the state began recovery.

A 4-year-old boy, three men and three women were among those who had died since the storms began Aug. 11, said Liz Woods, a spokesperson for the state Department of Homeland Security.

Among the latest confirmed victims was James Briar, a 31-year-old cyclist found dead early Sunday in a hole that opened up on a washed-out road in Henry County, east of Indianapolis. Henry County Coroner Brian Clark said Briar appears to have gone around a barricade and fallen into the collapsed road in New Castle. His body was discovered just before 4 a.m. Aug. 16 and he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Other victims included Matthew Morey, 19, of Delaware County, who drowned in the Mississinewa River, and a 58-year-old woman in Delaware County whose home was struck when a tree came through her bedroom window during the storm.

President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Indiana on Saturday, which allows the Federal Emergency Management Agency to provide resources to the state after severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes and flooding that swept over half of the state's 92 counties.

Heavy rain pushed the White River to a crest of approximately 24.60 feet in Hamilton County around 3:30 a.m. Aug. 15, breaking a record set more than 100 years ago, county officials said.

At the peak of the flooding, more than 350,000 residents lost power, including almost all of Lake County, and the Indiana National Guard was deployed to assist local responders.
</article>

A 4-year-old boy, three men and three women were among those who had died since the storms began Aug. 11, said Liz Woods, a spokesperson for the state Department of Homeland Security.

Among the latest confirmed victims was James Briar, a 31-year-old cyclist found dead early Sunday in a hole that opened up on a washed-out road in Henry County, east of Indianapolis. Henry County Coroner Brian Clark said Briar appears to have gone around a barricade and fallen into the collapsed road in New Castle. His body was discovered just before 4 a.m. Aug. 16 and he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Other victims included Matthew Morey, 19, of Delaware County, who drowned in the Mississinewa River, and a 58-year-old woman in Delaware County whose home was struck when a tree came through her bedroom window during the storm.

President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Indiana on Saturday, which allows the Federal Emergency Management Agency to provide resources to the state after severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes and flooding that swept over half of the state's 92 counties.

Heavy rain pushed the White River to a crest of approximately 24.60 feet in Hamilton County around 3:30 a.m. Aug. 15, breaking a record set more than 100 years ago, county officials said.

At the peak of the flooding, more than 350,000 residents lost power, including almost all of Lake County, and the Indiana National Guard was deployed to assist local responders.
</article>

<article>
Somali Airlines to resume flights after 35-year hiatus

MOGADISHU — Somalia's national carrier, Somali Airlines, is expected to resume flights in September 2026, more than three decades after it stopped operating following the collapse of the country's central government in 1991.

Ahmed Moalin, director of the Somali Civil Aviation Authority, said Saturday that preparations to relaunch the carrier had been completed and that flights were expected to begin next month.

"Somali Airlines is in the final stage," Moalin said. "I think the first flight will begin in September."

Somali Airlines, established in 1964 and once known as the "White Star," was the country's flag carrier, operating domestic and international routes, before its operations were halted by the civil war that followed the ouster of President Siad Barre in 1991.

The planned revival follows several earlier missed restart targets. The government announced an agreement involving two Airbus A320 aircraft in July 2025 as the first step toward reviving the carrier, and in October 2025 the transport ministry said the airline would begin services by the end of that year. That did not happen.

Mogadishu's Aden Adde International Airport is currently served by international carriers including Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways and Turkish Airlines, and for more than 30 years air travel in Somalia has largely been handled by private and foreign airlines.

Officials say the return of the national carrier is meant to improve domestic and regional connectivity, strengthen links with the Somali diaspora, create jobs and support trade.
</article>

Ahmed Moalin, director of the Somali Civil Aviation Authority, said Saturday that preparations to relaunch the carrier had been completed and that flights were expected to begin next month.

"Somali Airlines is in the final stage," Moalin said. "I think the first flight will begin in September."

Somali Airlines, established in 1964 and once known as the "White Star," was the country's flag carrier, operating domestic and international routes, before its operations were halted by the civil war that followed the ouster of President Siad Barre in 1991.

The planned revival follows several earlier missed restart targets. The government announced an agreement involving two Airbus A320 aircraft in July 2025 as the first step toward reviving the carrier, and in October 2025 the transport ministry said the airline would begin services by the end of that year. That did not happen.

Mogadishu's Aden Adde International Airport is currently served by international carriers including Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways and Turkish Airlines, and for more than 30 years air travel in Somalia has largely been handled by private and foreign airlines.

Officials say the return of the national carrier is meant to improve domestic and regional connectivity, strengthen links with the Somali diaspora, create jobs and support trade.
</article>

Somali Airlines to resume flights after 35-year hiatus

MOGADISHU — Somalia's national carrier, Somali Airlines, is expected to resume flights in September 2026, more than three decades after it stopped operating following the collapse of the country's central government in 1991.

Ahmed Moalin, director of the Somali Civil Aviation Authority, said Saturday that preparations to relaunch the carrier had been completed and that flights were expected to begin next month.

"Somali Airlines is in the final stage," Moalin said. "I think the first flight will begin in September."

Somali Airlines, established in 1964 and once known as the "White Star," was the country's flag carrier, operating domestic and international routes, before its operations were halted by the civil war that followed the ouster of President Siad Barre in 1991.

The planned revival follows several earlier missed restart targets. The government announced an agreement involving two Airbus A320 aircraft in July 2025 as the first step toward reviving the carrier, and in October 2025 the transport ministry said the airline would begin services by the end of that year. That did not happen.

Mogadishu's Aden Adde International Airport is currently served by international carriers including Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways and Turkish Airlines, and for more than 30 years air travel in Somalia has largely been handled by private and foreign airlines.

Officials say the return of the national carrier is meant to improve domestic and regional connectivity, strengthen links with the Somali diaspora, create jobs and support trade.

The regulator also pointed to a product change in early March, when Discord introduced end-to-end encryption to its communications, making the company's access to in-stream content even more limited.

Discord faces fines of up to 50 million reais (about $9.67 million) per violation.

<article>
TikTok pays $400 million in US children's privacy settlement

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance on Friday agreed to a $400 million settlement to resolve the US Justice Department's lawsuit alleging the short-video app violated children's online privacy.

Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered in 2019 with the Federal Trade Commission against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly.

The settlement represents one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a case under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, a federal law enacted in 2000 that requires services directed at children to obtain parental consent before collecting personal information from users under age 13.

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit in 2024 in the US District Court for the Central District of California, on referral from the Federal Trade Commission. The suit accused TikTok and ByteDance of collecting vast amounts of data on millions of users under 13, failing to honor requests from parents who wanted their children's accounts deleted, and not deleting accounts even when the companies knew they belonged to children under 13.

As part of the 2019 consent decree, Musical.ly had paid a $5.7 million fine for COPPA violations.

The justice department said that since it sued the platform, TikTok has "undergone significant changes," including to its ownership, privacy practices and platform controls for young users. The settlement involves TikTok's operations in China.

COPPA is also the law that dozens of US states are now suing Meta over.
</article>

KUALA LUMPUR (Reuters) — Malaysia's Johor Darul Ta'zim (JDT) set a new world record on Friday, extending their unbeaten run in top-flight league football to 109 matches after a 3-0 victory over Kuching City in the opening match of the 2026/27 Malaysian Super League season.

Marcos Guilherme scored in the 11th minute, and Oscar Arribas and Shahab Zahedi found the net in the second half as the 12-time defending champions won in front of a packed crowd at Sultan Ibrahim Stadium.

The win took JDT one game clear of the previous mark of 108 top-flight league games without defeat, set by Ivory Coast's ASEC Mimosas between 1989 and 1994. JDT had matched that record in May with a 14-1 demolition of Kelantan The Real Warriors, the biggest winning margin in the league's history, in the final match of last season.

The Southern Tigers have not lost a league match since a 1-0 defeat by Terengganu in April 2021, and have gone unbeaten through the last four Super League campaigns. In the run's only serious scare, they came from 2-1 down against Sri Pahang in May 2022 before all-time record scorer Bergson levelled in the 88th minute.

The club is owned by Johor Crown Prince Tunku Ismail, whose arrival more than a decade ago set the team on its path of dominance, and is managed by the Spanish coach Xisco Munoz.

JDT were also drawn 3-3 against Chelsea in a preseason friendly this summer, and remain the only Southeast Asian club to have won the AFC Cup, in 2015.

Kenya helicopter crash kills seven, including Ecuador's intelligence chief

NAIROBI (AFP) — All seven people on board a safari helicopter, six passengers and a pilot, were killed on Wednesday when the aircraft crashed in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe in Samburu County, central Kenya, authorities said.

Kenya's Civil Aviation Authority said the group's Eurocopter EC130 B4, operated by Lady Lori Helicopters, crashed at 9:13 a.m. (06:13 GMT) after departing the Loisaba Conservancy on a scenic charter toward the Ewaso Ng'iro area. The Kenya Red Cross said difficult terrain and a fire at the crash site hampered search and recovery efforts.

Among the dead were Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, director general of Ecuador's strategic intelligence center, and his wife, Stephany Hollihan, 42, a fashion designer who also held US citizenship.

A US State Department spokesperson said five of the six passengers killed were US citizens, and NBC News reported that one of them was Jose Suarez, a prominent television executive. The other American victims were from South Florida.

Sensi-Contugi, a former businessman and close associate of Ecuador's right-wing President Daniel Noboa, was appointed head of national intelligence in January 2024. Noboa declared three days of national mourning and ordered a state funeral.

The pilot was identified as Josh Outram, an American.

Mount Ololokwe is a sacred mountain for the Samburu people, its summit rising 2,000 metres above sea level, and it is a popular hiking destination where companies offer helicopter flyovers.

DAMASCUS (Reuters) — The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, lifting what Damascus says was the last major barrier to private-sector investment in the country as Washington deepens ties to the new Syrian government.

The removal, posted on the U.S. Treasury's website, took effect after a 45-day congressional review period triggered when President Donald Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the decades-old designation. Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting armed groups, and it remained throughout the rule of his son, Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa in December 2024.

" These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

Monday's announcement also revoked the designation of al-Nusrah Front, the group formerly led by al-Sharaa and known as Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a global terrorist organization. HTS was once al-Qaeda's official branch in Syria. The move leaves Cuba, North Korea and Iran as the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.

Trump notified Congress after meeting al-Sharaa in Ankara in July, telling the Syrian president in a letter that he had promised to remove all barriers preventing Syria from rebuilding.

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said there is "no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," and the country's central bank chief, Safwat Raslan, said the government is building a modern financial system.

US envoy Tom Barrack called the end of the designation a decisive step in Syria's journey "from isolation to partnership."

France's top court blocks social media ban for under-15s

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

The law would have barred children younger than 15 from opening a social media account from September 1, and platforms would have had to close existing accounts within four months using age verification approved by the French privacy regulator. French lawmakers approved the ban in July, which would have made France the first European country to enact such a measure, after Australia barred under-16s from platforms including Facebook, TikTok and YouTube in December.

The council said that by prohibiting minors under 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them, and the legislature did not establish the conditions and limits of that proof. It also said the ban's scope was too broad, reaching collaboration tools, communication apps and social games whose risks for minors are not established.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

The law would have barred children younger than 15 from opening a social media account from September 1, and platforms would have had to close existing accounts within four months using age verification approved by the French privacy regulator. French lawmakers approved the ban in July, which would have made France the first European country to enact such a measure, after Australia barred under-16s from platforms including Facebook, TikTok and YouTube in December.

The council said that by prohibiting minors under 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them, and the legislature did not establish the conditions and limits of that proof. It also said the ban's scope was too broad, reaching collaboration tools, communication apps and social games whose risks for minors are not established.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.
